newsitem.title: KENYA: Gunmen kill 17 students, Belgian nun in Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Gunmen kill 17 students, Belgian nun in Rwanda.

text.p: Militiamen massacred 17 schoolgirls and a Belgian nun and wounded 14 other girls in attacks on two schools in northwestern Rwanda on Monday, state radio said.
Rwanda's state news agency said an unspecified number of civilians living near one school were also massacred.
The agency said the militiamen burst into a dormitory of a school at Muramkba in Satinskyi commune in Gisenyi province and asked children to separate by ethnic and regional background.
The agency, monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation, quoted survivors as saying the students refused to divide themselves and the gunmen opened fire indisciminately.
"When they attempted to attack the second school, the army intervened, but the marauding gang had already killed the nun," said the agency.
It identified the dead Belgian as 62-year-old teacher Griet Bosmans, who lived in Rwanda since 1960.
In Brussels, a Belgian foreign ministry spokesman confirmed the nun, who was the school headmistress, and a number of children were killed when armed men attacked early on Monday.
He said indications were that she was not killed because she was white but because she was a member of the school staff.
State radio said security forces captured one of the suspected attackers and were trying to track down the others.
The agency did not identify the attackers but Rwandan authorities have blamed Hutu militiamen for a series of attacks in the western part of the country this year.

Three Spanish aid workers were shot dead by gunmen in the northwestern town of Ruhengeri in January, followed by a Canadian priest at Sunday mass in Ruhengeri province in early February and a Briton, a Cambodian and two Rwandan U.N. human rights monitors in an ambush in the southwest the same month.

Rwandan authorities say the attacks come from former Hutu Rwandan troops and Interahamwe militiamen who returned to Rwanda from Tanzania with refugees late last year and who led the genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates in 1994.
Rwanda this month refused to allow U.N. agencies to fly Hutu refugees back direct to Kigali from Zaire, saying they posed a security threat at the main airport in the capital.
But the U.N. refugee agency said on Monday Rwanda agreed to such flights after up to 100,000 refugees fled into the jungle south of the northeast Zairean capital of Kisangani last week.
Laurent Kabila, leader of the Tutsi-dominated rebels in Zaire, has given U.N. agencies 60 days from May 1 to repatriate all the estimated 350,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees still in Zaire.
Rwanda's jails and lockups are already overcrowded with 100,000 Hutus accused of involvement in the genocide in 1994.
